journal_name: Journal of Computer and System Sciences

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces the Temporal-Graph Turing Machine (TGTM), a novel computational model that fundamentally reconceptualizes computation over dynamically evolving network structures. Unlike traditional models that treat network topology as static, the TGTM incorporates time as a first-class computational resource, allowing information to propagate along temporal paths that respect both spatial connectivity and temporal ordering constraints. We establish a comprehensive complexity theory for this model, defining相应的 complexity类并证明其与已知计算模型的关系。Our main theoretical contribution demonstrates that the TGTM introduces a strictly larger complexity class than polynomial-time Turing machines, with specific decision problems exhibiting exponential computational advantages under the new model. We further establish connections to automata theory by characterizing TGTM-recognizable languages through novel temporal regular expressions. The framework enables analysis of computational complexity in dynamic networks including mobile ad hoc networks, blockchain protocols, and distributed ledger systems where timing constraints fundamentally affect computability. This work opens new research directions by establishing the theoretical foundations for what can and cannot be computed when resource availability varies over time, providing essential tools for understanding the inherent limitations of algorithms operating in truly dynamic environments.

We establish significantly improved lower bounds on the communication complexity required for computing arbitrary functions over quantum networks where entanglement resources are limited. Prior work established that any protocol achieving bounded-error quantum communication requires at least Ω(√n) qubits for certain promise problems. We substantially tighten this bound to Ω(n^(1/2) · log n), demonstrating that the previous results substantially underestimated the communication requirements in entangled network settings. Our lower bound proof combines information-theoretic methods with novel entropic uncertainty relations specifically tailored to network topologies with bounded connectivity. The technical contribution involves a refined analysis of quantum information decoupling in multi-user scenarios, yielding implications for distributed computing, secure multi-party computation, and network coding. We further show that our lower bounds are tight by constructing explicit protocols achieving the new bounds, thereby characterizing the exact quantum communication complexity landscape for this class of problems. The improved bounds have direct applications to the design of efficient quantum networking protocols and provide stronger impossibility results for device-independent quantum cryptography in realistic settings with limited entanglement distribution.

We present a novel architecture for Byzantine fault-tolerant state machine replication that fundamentally reconceptualizes the traditional assumption of static adversarial thresholds. Existing protocols assume a fixed bound on the number of malicious nodes determined at system initialization, creating a rigid security model inadequate for dynamic real-world deployments. Our Behavioral-Trust Consensus (BTC) framework introduces a dynamic trust model where node reliability is continuously assessed through cryptographic attestations of protocol-compliant behavior, enabling adaptive security guarantees that evolve with actual system dynamics. The architecture implements a novel reputation mechanism with provable convergence properties, allowing the system to dynamically adjust its tolerance thresholds based on observed node behavior over time. We prove that BTC achieves safety and liveness in partially synchronous networks even when the adversary adaptively corrupts nodes, provided the total corruption budget is spread non-concentrated across the system lifetime. The protocol achieves agreement in O(t) expected rounds with O(n log n) message complexity, where t reflects the current threshold based on behavioral assessment. Implementation and evaluation on geographically distributed testbeds demonstrate practical performance, with throughput exceeding 10,000 transactions per second while maintaining robust security under adaptive attacks that would compromise traditional static-threshold protocols.

We design and analyze an efficient protocol for achieving atomic commitment in geo-distributed database systems that significantly improves upon existing solutions in both message complexity and coordinator-free operation. Current two-phase commit variants suffer from blocking behavior under coordinator failures or require expensive view changes, while existing crash-tolerant alternatives incur prohibitive message overheads of O(n²) in wide-area settings. Our Lattice-Partition Commit (LPC) protocol achieves coordinator-free atomic commitment through a novel combination of lattice-structured metadata and partition-aware agreement phases. The protocol reduces message complexity to O(n log n) in the common case while guaranteeing non-blocking operation under a majority of correct partitions. We provide formal correctness proofs using TLA+ specifications and establish that LPC satisfies all ACID properties with probability 1 in partially synchronous executions. Evaluation on a 64-node distributed database prototype spanning three geographic regions demonstrates 47% reduction in commit latency compared to standard two-phase commit and maintains throughput within 12% of non-transactional baseline operations. The protocol introduces only negligible overhead in storage complexity, requiring O(log n) additional metadata per participant. These improvements make LPC particularly suitable for emerging geo-distributed ledger applications requiring strong consistency guarantees with minimal coordination overhead.
